{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-mt-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"b7c46a0f6f81d1c84293026c30a161cd435d8d43c4869cc408b77d656debf297","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-mt-class-d:lineage:50","source_registry_sha256":"35425fc1b75886d4bce9129f5de9443ae8cee634cff4a62363bbcd7cc017fe32","source_liveness_sha256":"bf7b5d7e97593e3a1c6181f4785c9171cedac6e24ab65da907a644a4b4907add"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Driver fitness and impairment","heading":"C — Driver fitness and impairment","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Driver fitness and impairment

FACT_ID: sec12-F01 | anchor: A01
Montana requires a vision test before issuing a driver license. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F02 | anchor: A01
The stated vision standard is at least 20/40 in one eye or better, with or without corrective lenses. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F03 | anchor: A01
Wear required glasses or contact lenses whenever driving, even on a short trip. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F04 | anchor: A01
Driving without corrective lenses required by the license can result in a citation. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F05 | anchor: A01
Keep spare glasses in the vehicle in case the usual pair is lost or broken. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F06 | anchor: A01
Avoid dark glasses or tinted contacts at night because they reduce the light available for seeing. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F07 | anchor: A01
Side vision helps detect hazards, but mirrors and a sideways glance may still be needed to see them clearly. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F08 | anchor: A01
Judging vehicle speeds and distances takes practice, especially for merging gaps and two-lane passing. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F09 | anchor: A01
If night vision is difficult, limit nighttime driving to what is necessary and drive cautiously when it is unavoidable. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F10 | anchor: A01
Horns, sirens and screeching tires can give an audible warning of danger. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F11 | anchor: A01
A driver with hearing loss can adapt by relying more on vision and staying alert. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec12-F12 | anchor: A02
Fatigue can reduce vision and alertness, slow decisions and make falling asleep at the wheel more likely. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F13 | anchor: A02
Begin a long trip rested after a normal night’s sleep rather than leaving already tired. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F14 | anchor: A02
Before leaving, eat lightly instead of a large meal that may cause sleepiness. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F15 | anchor: A02
On a long trip, stop for a break about every two hours or whenever a break is needed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F16 | anchor: A02
Allow enough time to complete a trip without rushing. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F17 | anchor: A02
Avoid driving late at night when that is normally your sleeping time. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F18 | anchor: A02
Do not drive while sleepy; stop to sleep or share the driving with another driver when possible. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F19 | anchor: A02
Alcohol impairs judgment, reflexes, reaction time, clear vision and alertness needed for driving. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F20 | anchor: A02
If you drink alcohol, do not drive, because even a single beverage can affect driving. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F21 | anchor: A02
The amount and pace of drinking, body weight, food and general health can all affect impairment. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F22 | anchor: A02
Alcohol can accumulate even when someone consumes only one drink per hour. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F23 | anchor: A02
The handbook’s drink comparison uses one and one-half ounces of 80-proof liquor, twelve ounces of commercial beer or five ounces of wine. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F24 | anchor: A02
Craft beer and specialty drinks can contain more alcohol than the standard drink examples. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F25 | anchor: A02
Arrange for a designated driver who does not drink, or use available public transportation or a cab. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec12-F26 | anchor: A03
Driving at a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08 percent or more, or while under the influence, can lead to arrest. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F27 | anchor: A03
Blood alcohol concentration describes the proportion of alcohol in blood and is usually assessed by breath, blood or urine testing. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F28 | anchor: A03
Refusing a police-requested blood alcohol test can result in loss of the driver license. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F29 | anchor: A03
An open alcoholic beverage container must not be unlawfully kept in a vehicle’s highway passenger area. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F30 | anchor: A03
A locked glove compartment or storage compartment is among the listed permitted places for an alcoholic beverage container. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F31 | anchor: A03
The handbook lists a trunk, luggage compartment, truck bed or cargo compartment as permitted container-storage locations. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F32 | anchor: A03
In a vehicle without a trunk, an alcoholic container may be behind the last upright seat or in a closed container in an area not normally occupied by riders. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F33 | anchor: A03
The container restriction has an exception for an unbroken seal with none of the original contents removed. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F34 | anchor: A03
The listed open-container exceptions include storage in the living quarters of a camper, travel trailer or motor home. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F35 | anchor: A03
Passengers carried by a hired driver in a bus, taxi or limousine have a listed open-container exception. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F36 | anchor: A03
To report suspected impaired driving, contact local law enforcement or the highway patrol with the vehicle description and direction of travel. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec12-F37 | anchor: A03
A person reporting suspected drunk driving does not have to provide a name. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0082]

Misconceptions: Feeling alert does not prove unimpaired driving, and a numerical alcohol threshold does not authorize driving while under the influence.
Mnemonics: Authored cue: see clearly, stay rested, check medicines, choose a sober ride.
Glossary: Corrective lenses; fatigue; blood alcohol concentration; designated driver; open container; physician attestation.
Dynamic facts: Current alcohol-law exceptions, penalty amounts, reporting contacts and medical licensing applicability require current official evidence; individual fitness is not inferred from age alone.
